text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- The government's decision to raise taxes on petrol will not bring in as much tax revenue as was hoped as consumers counteract higher prices by using less, a commentator writes.

- Higher tax on petrol is especially painful for those whose only alternative is driving their own car to work. Robert Grahn, who lives 70 km from his employer SSAB in Lulea, a northern Swedish town, will pay 2,000 crowns more annually because of the new tax.

- Swedish second quarter gross domestic product (GDP) grew more than expected -- 2.3 percent compared with the second quarter of 1996. Private consumption and exports have increased but unemployment continues to be high.
- One third of employers perform regular drug testing to combat increased misuse. Almost half of new employees at large Swedish companies, or 45 percent, are tested for drug use when they are hired.

- Swedish banking shares rose after false rumours that commercial banks S-E-Banken and Handelsbanken would merge. Neither one of the banks would comment on the rumours. Restructuring expected in financial markets ahead of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) is causing constant rumours about banking mergers to spring up.

- Swedish appliance retail store OnOff bought rival stores in the Axling group and Ljud & Bild to make itself the largest Swedish home electronics company by turnover. The new company will have 57 stores concentrated in Sweden's largest cities.

- Swedish investment group Investor AB managed to post a good result for the first half of 1997 despite weak development for drug company Astra , with the civil aviation part within Saab AB and carmaker Saab Automobile , all of which it has holdings.
- Sweden will give Poland 125 million crowns in aid to help victims of flood damage.

- Swedish railroad operator SJ only allows the country's main taxi companies to wait for customers near the central train stations. Smaller taxi companies protested when Sweden's civil aviation administration tried to introduce a similar system near the airport in Swedish west coast city, Gothenburg.

- The banking sector index has risen over 90 percent in one year on rumours of a merger in the sector as well as falling interest rates and expectations for high profits in the sector. The index rose 5.5 percent on Thursday, with S-E-Banken leading, jumping over seven percent.

- Swedish insurance companies are taking advantage of high share prices and selling off parts of their portfolios. Net sales of stocks by insurers totalled over 11.6 billion crowns in the second quarter.
- Volvo's truck division, which has seen profits fall in recent years, will launch a new line of vehicles in 1998, newspaper sources say.

- Telia Overseas, the international division of Swedish state-owned public telephone company, is leading one of five consortiums tendering for a license to operate a mobile telephone network in Sao Paulo. The Brazilian government says it will not consider a bid for less than 4.5 billion crowns.
- The U.S. Discovery Channel will film the eight-day Stockholm Water Festival, which begins today, organisers say.
